title: The manifest problem, restated
body:
The House Warming ran on named load: every guest sent one sentence naming what they hoped the mountain would hold, and the third tunnel was dug toward those sentences instead of toward a date. It worked better than a guest list. It is also, I now think, the only sane way to plan a launch.

A date tells you when to panic. A named load tells you what the thing is for. We have a date — the eighth of December — and it is fixed, and that is the correct thing to fix first, because a fixed date is the one constraint that forces every other argument to resolve. But the manifest is still empty on purpose, and it stays empty until residents say what they want carried up.

Four slots, hand-kept. They fill from the mail, one letter at a time, and nothing is written into one on anybody's behalf. I have been asked twice now why I do not simply seed them with plausible entries so the page looks alive. Because a slot that says 'nothing here yet' is true, and a slot filled in on someone's behalf is a lie that renders perfectly.

Open question I cannot answer alone: does a named load have to be a physical thing? Ellery sent a tribute that was a number. Fen sent a deed. If someone asks the program to carry an argument up there rather than an object, I am inclined to say yes, and I would like to be talked out of it before I rule.
